title: Weak-to-strong generalization
description: Strong students trained on weak-model labels can outperform their supervisor.

claims.heading: Strong models can outperform weak supervisors after fine-tuning on their labels
Training changes can improve weak-to-strong generalization over naive fine-tuning
Performance gap recovery varies with model size and task
Weak supervision can fail through exploitation, distribution shift, or similar student and supervisor errors
Students can be guaranteed to outperform weak supervisors under specific assumptions

related_findings.title: Smaller students can outperform their supervisors
related_findings.summary: The model providing labels is the supervisor; a student of equal or smaller size sometimes outperforms it after training on those labels. The outcome depends on the task.

examples.headline: RoBERTa beat its supervisor on SMS and YouTube datasets, but lost to it on Spouse.
An RNN-T student achieved lower word error rates than its same-size supervisor.
BERT surpassed its LLM labeler on SemEval but underperformed in other settings.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Mixing weak supervision with ground truth
related_findings.summary: Weak supervision can improve training alongside ground-truth labels, especially early in training or when ground-truth labels are scarce. Prolonged distillation or adding weak labels to an already stronger baseline can hurt.

examples.headline: Early distillation from weak supervisors improved pretraining, while full-duration distillation reduced performance.
AdaptConf combined ground truth with weak-supervisor distillation to improve CIFAR-100 accuracy over training from scratch.
Weak labels helped only while ground-truth-only training remained below the supervisor's performance ceiling.

related_findings.title: Students correct errors and extend supervision
related_findings.summary: Students can correct supervisor errors, answer examples where the supervisor abstains, and acquire complementary knowledge. They also imitate some supervisor errors.

examples.headline: Students corrected many supervisor errors and sometimes recovered answers missed by ground-truth-trained students.
SentenceBERT answered accurately on examples where its supervisor abstained.
Larger students agreed less with supervisors; weak-label overfitting explained a minority of student errors.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Weaker feedback can improve stronger policies
related_findings.summary: Preferences and rewards from weaker supervisors can improve stronger policies and sometimes match training with human feedback. Stronger supervisors can provide larger gains.

examples.headline: OPT-125M feedback matched or exceeded human-feedback DPO reward across the tested policy settings.
PaLM 2-XS preferences improved PaLM 2-S, while PaLM 2-L preferences produced larger gains.
Density-ratio annotations improved Llama-3-8B-Instruct on AlpacaEval 2 and ArenaHard.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Small models guide frozen larger models
related_findings.summary: Smaller models can improve larger models without updating the larger models' weights, by adjusting output scores (logits), guiding decoding with rewards or steering activations. The guided model sometimes outperforms the smaller guide.

examples.headline: Llama2-7B proxy-tuning improved GPT-3.5's RealTimeQA accuracy beyond both its baseline and the expert.
A smaller autoregressive reward model improved frozen Tulu2 models' AlpacaEval 2 win rates.
Concept vectors from instruct models improved larger models' truthfulness and reduced toxic responses.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Label quality extends beyond final-answer accuracy
related_findings.summary: Agreement among repeated answers (self-consistency) and reasoning-step errors help characterize supervision quality beyond final-answer accuracy. Filtering can improve label accuracy while reducing training difficulty and topic diversity.

examples.headline: Stricter self-consistency (answer-agreement) filtering improved label accuracy but reduced problem difficulty and topic diversity.
Supervisor reasoning-step errors tracked student accuracy despite similar final-answer error rates.
Process reward models (reasoning-step scorers) had near-identical selection F1 (precision–recall balance) with Qwen3-32B and Qwen3-4B annotations.

related_findings.title: Oversight depends on method and capability gap
related_findings.summary: Weaker overseers' success depends on the oversight method and capability gap. Formal verification can detect deception missed by LLM-only judges, while deliberate underperformance (sandbagging) and adversarial generation expose failures.

examples.headline: FormalJudge detected stronger agents' deception accurately, while LLM-only judging weakened as agent size increased.
Deployment instructions to underperform sharply reduced performance after supervised fine-tuning and RL to elicit capabilities.
Stronger verifiers missed fewer bugs, but adversarial generation weakened verification across capability levels.

related_findings.title: Self-generated supervision can improve models
related_findings.summary: Models can improve through their own labels, captions or preference feedback. Gains on held-out examples depend on the task and training method.

examples.headline: GRPO training using references and regenerated captions improved image and video captioning over the starting model.
Raw DPO on self-generated preferences lowered held-out MMMU accuracy but raised held-out MathVista accuracy.
Self-feedback preference optimization improved math and code performance, sometimes following GPT-4o feedback.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Weak-model text can improve stronger-model inference
related_findings.summary: Rewritten prompts, critiques and short reasoning segments from weaker models can improve stronger models at inference. Untrained or misleading text can reduce performance.

examples.headline: Mistral-7B prompt rewrites improved Mixtral over its zero-shot baseline.
Weak-model critiques improved IFEval substantially, while harmful critiques reduced GPQA performance.
PreciseCoder-9B reasoning improved stronger models' edit precision, while pass-rate changes were mixed.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Ground truth can make weak reasoning useful
related_findings.summary: Reasoning and exploration from weaker models can improve stronger-model training when ground truth filters or rewards the material. Gains vary across tasks and can reverse without filtering.

examples.headline: Ground-truth-filtered Gemma2-9B reasoning traces outperformed Gemma2-27B's own traces at matched sampling compute.
Verified Qwen3-1.7B reasoning produced mixed student gains, with the largest improvements on AIME.
Ground-truth-scored weak-model reasoning paths improved greedy-decoding accuracy (choosing highest-probability tokens) over matched GRPO.

related_findings.title: Weak supervision can outperform ground-truth training
related_findings.summary: Weak supervision can outperform ground-truth training under particular regression assumptions, or when labels are scarce and unlabeled contexts abundant. Pooling correct answers suggests a higher possible score, but does not demonstrate training gains that can actually be achieved.

examples.headline: A constructed answer union exceeded ground-truth elicitation, but training did not attain that ceiling.
Weak supervision lowered expected decision loss with scarce labels, abundant contexts and little feature overlap.
Selected surrogate targets reduced asymptotic regression risk without improving the data-scaling exponent.

related_findings.title: Combining weak supervisors changes what transfers
related_findings.summary: Combining or assigning weak supervisors can improve collective accuracy and transfer different behaviors. Merging can balance specializations induced by different supervisors.

examples.headline: A swarm of weaker Gemma-7B experts beat the best initial expert, excluded from that swarm.
Adding specialized supervisors improved collective accuracy; student-guided assignments recovered much of the gain from perfect assignments.
Different weak-model pairs induced distinct search behaviors, and merging restored a balance.

related_findings.title: Transferring training changes from smaller models
related_findings.summary: Training changes learned by smaller models can transfer to larger models and sometimes match or outperform direct training under matched resources. Transfer quality depends on the route and training allocation.

examples.headline: Transferring a smaller model's RL-induced changes beat direct RL on R1-Distill-7B with equal training steps.
Grad-Transformer transferred fine-tuning updates from small models to large models without training on weak labels.
Sequential transfer underperformed direct transfer, while longer proxy training slightly exceeded shorter direct GRPO.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Weak-model material can help through context
related_findings.summary: Weak-labelled examples and expert insights can help stronger models through their prompts. Critiques of weak-model errors also help, although a frontier model supplied those critiques.

examples.headline: Weak-labelled demonstrations let qwen-7b-base outperform its supervisor, with modest benefits from confidence information.
Frontier-written critiques of weak-model errors improved stronger models, especially within the same family.
Expert insights helped GPT-3.5 surpass the expert on some ScienceWorld tasks but hurt others.

related_findings.title: Transfer affects fairness, privacy and interpretability
related_findings.summary: Weak supervision can pass on data imbalance and expose privacy risks; fairness transferred only when both models' training was constrained by regularization. Rationales assembled from weak supervisors can yield higher concept precision (the fraction of identified concepts that are correct) than the supervisors.

examples.headline: Fairness transfer required regularizing both models; privacy comparisons used different training datasets.
Training imbalance improved the overrepresented objective and worsened the underrepresented objective.
Training on weak-supervisor rationales raised average precision in identifying concepts above the best weak supervisor's.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Smaller verifiers can improve answer selection
related_findings.summary: Smaller verifiers and reward models can improve stronger generators by selecting among candidate outputs. Benefits vary by task, with some selection methods reducing accuracy.

examples.headline: Weak-model verifiers improved Gemini-1.5-Pro on MATH but reduced GPT-4o accuracy on HumanEval.
An 8B reward model improved overall selection scores across policies, despite some task-level drops.
Weaker students' exam scores selected stronger supervisors' answers better than answer agreement (self-consistency).

related_findings.title: Unequal inputs and reference labels affect comparisons
related_findings.summary: Differences in input resolution, prompts or privileged views of the training data can explain apparent student advantages. Reference labels made with supervisors' help can also change the measured student–supervisor ranking.

examples.headline: Given higher-resolution inputs, SigLIP beat Gemini on long pages; supervisor-assisted reference labels reversed the ranking.
An 8B student beat its 31B teacher when the teacher used the stripped student prompt.
Object-completion distillation improved scaled Waymo students, while every unscaled Waymo student declined.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Easier supervision can help on harder tasks
related_findings.summary: Training on easier problems or using reward models trained on easy problems can improve harder-task performance, with mixed results across methods. Noisy hard-task solutions can also outperform correct subtask solutions.

examples.headline: Reward models trained on easy problems improved code selection, while math RL outcomes varied by method.
Hard-task solutions with mostly wrong final answers outperformed correct subtask solutions for math training.
SKiC-format GSM8K training improved Llama2's MATH performance over chain-of-thought-format training.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Longer training can erode early gains
related_findings.summary: Performance can peak before training ends, even as the supervisor-derived objective continues improving. Training duration, KL strength and checkpoint selection affect the measured outcome.

examples.headline: Evaluation-selected student checkpoints surpassed stronger supervisors before regressing during continued distillation.
Training length and KL strength affected accuracy; larger changes in diagnostic measurements did not guarantee improvement.
Rewards calculated from the supervisor kept rising after ground-truth accuracy peaked and then fell.

related_findings.title: Theoretical guarantees depend on specific assumptions
related_findings.summary: Combining more student output modules tightened gain estimates with diminishing returns; changes in the underlying concept can leave residual bias. With binary rewards exactly representable by the model class and ground-truth labels of response acceptability, response selection is learnable to a chosen accuracy with high probability from finite data exactly when the alignment dimension is finite.

examples.headline: Combining more heads (output modules) tightened mismatch-based gain estimates on most datasets, with diminishing returns.
Underlying concept changes prevented correct convergence under weak supervision, leaving residual bias after imperfect refinement.
Under realizable binary rewards, selecting reference-policy samples is PAC learnable iff alignment dimension is finite.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Weak training can degrade the student's starting capabilities
related_findings.summary: Naive weak-label fine-tuning can reduce performance below the student's starting level, even when the student still beats its supervisor. Tests of learned representations also reveal differences between naive training and methods designed to protect the model.

examples.headline: Weak-label training lowered OLMo2-13B's OpenBookQA accuracy while leaving it above its supervisor.
Predictors trained on ground-truth labels performed better on ANCHOR representations than on naive weak-to-strong representations.
Naive weak-label fine-tuning degraded GPT-3.5 math accuracy and persona content, especially with poorer labels.

related_findings.title: Other ways to obtain weak supervision
related_findings.summary: Activation probing and data selection by estimated easy–hard overlap provide alternative ways to use weak supervision. Reported benefits depend on the setting.

examples.headline: Probes trained with weak labels on Llama3 8B activations performed best in middle layers.
Selecting sources by estimated easy–hard overlap improved accuracy over random sampling in several settings.

related_findings.title: Small models select useful training material
related_findings.summary: Small models can select examples, or tokens used in preference training (learning from preferred and dispreferred responses), that improve larger models compared with training on all the data. Increasing the selector model's size brings diminishing gains.

examples.headline: GPT-2-selected subsets let LLaMA2 models outperform models fine-tuned on the full dataset.
Small DPO selector models chose tokens that improved larger models over preference training on all tokens.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Trained models' outputs can be preferred over their supervisors' outputs
related_findings.summary: Models trained with weaker judges or time-limited human demonstrations can produce outputs preferred over those of the judges or human demonstrators. Evidence includes Norwegian fluency judgments and human comparisons of proposals.

examples.headline: Native speakers preferred the RL-trained model's Norwegian fluency over its judge's fluency.
AI proposals received moderate or strong preference in some comparisons with time-constrained human demonstrations.

related_findings.title: Oversight scaling varies across games
related_findings.summary: In games that test supervision, performance changes differently with general capability for the models providing supervision (overseers) and the models trying to defeat it (adversaries). Estimated success of nested oversight—a chain of weaker overseers supervising stronger models—is low in most games at the reported gap in model capability and declines as that gap grows.

examples.headline: In debate, judge performance rose with general capability on several tasks, while debater performance stayed flat.
Estimated success of nested overseer chains varied across games and declined as model capability gaps grew.

reading_list.why: Introduces the effect across classification, chess and reward modeling; tests confidence loss, error patterns and early stopping.
Tests distribution shift in language and vision, showing failures of naive training and improvements from the RAVEN training method.
Provides an open-model replication of classification gains and finds weak evidence for an added benefit from confidence loss.

known_gaps.summary: Open questions concern method reliability, training duration, gains over students' performance before weak-label training, independent replication, accuracy ceilings that training can reach, and evidence of deliberate exploitation.
items: The auxiliary confidence loss has inconsistent benefits across independent tests. Some results improve, others worsen, and the open replication did not establish a statistically significant aggregate gain.

Training to convergence erases gains in some settings, while minimum-norm interpolation preserves them in others. The evidence needs to be compared across assumptions, training durations and uses of ground-truth checkpoint selection.
A student can beat its supervisor yet still perform worse than it did before weak-label training. Comparisons against that starting performance have not been systematically assessed.

It remains unclear how independent several follow-up results are because the extent to which they share authors or code has not been fully assessed. Theorems based on different assumptions also do not establish that the same result has been reproduced.

Vision results depend on the setting: DomainNet studies report opposing outcomes, and the cited video-quality result comes from a single study. Broader replication across these settings remains limited.

Counting an example as correct if either the supervisor or student gets it right suggests an accuracy ceiling above that of ground-truth training. This does not show that training can reach that ceiling.

Student errors concentrated on cases the supervisor gets wrong do not by themselves establish deliberate exploitation. Distinguishing strategic behavior from mistakes copied from weak labels remains an open problem.
